title: the Alvars (Andal, Nammalvar)
hook: a silent boy under a tamarind tree, and a riddle that wakes him
carry: it will eat that, and lie there

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Alvars again: Andal's Tiruppavai, girls knocking on doors before dawn so nobody went to Krishna alone. Whose door did you knock on? Day nine hundred nine.

A man is walking south, following a light. That's how the story tells it: he's far away in the north, on pilgrimage, and he sees a glow in the southern sky that no one else seems to notice. He follows it for a long way. It leads him to a temple town in the Tamil country, to a tamarind tree, and to a young man sitting in a hollow at its foot. Eyes closed. Not speaking. People there say he has been that way since he was a baby. The traveler has one question for him, and it's a riddle.
screen: `A LIGHT IN THE SOUTHERN SKY.` → `A TAMARIND TREE.` → `A YOUNG MAN WHO NEVER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: The young man is Nammalvar, the second name in our title. The traveler is Madhurakavi. Tradition says Nammalvar was born and didn't cry, didn't nurse, didn't open his eyes, and his worried parents left him at the temple, where he sat under the tamarind, silent, growing up in stillness. Madhurakavi wants to know whether anyone is home behind those closed eyes. So he asks, roughly: if a small thing is born inside something dead, what will it eat, and where will it lie? And for the first time, the story says, Nammalvar answers. It will eat that, and it will lie there. That's it. Two short lines, and Madhurakavi falls at his feet and becomes his disciple for life. What did they mean? Here traditional readers give more than one answer. One traditional reading: the small thing is the living self, born into a body that is, by itself, lifeless matter. Until it turns to God, it feeds on that body's pleasures and pains, and stays there. Other teachers take the riddle further, or differently. The tradition keeps the riddle and lets it stay a little open. Then the silent one starts to sing. The songs that follow, gathered as the Tiruvaymoli, are full of longing for Vishnu. In some, he speaks as a girl pining for her absent lover, and her mother and friends speak about her. Sri Vaishnava tradition holds these songs so high it calls them the Tamil Veda. And Madhurakavi? He is remembered among the Alvars too, for a short poem in praise of no one but his teacher. A man who walked a long way after a light, and found it sitting very still.
screen: `A CHILD WHO NEVER CRIED.` · `THE RIDDLE: WHAT WILL IT EAT?` · `IT WILL EAT THAT, AND LIE THERE.` · `THE SILENT ONE BEGINS TO SING.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes close, or rest them low, like the young man under the tree. Sit still enough that your body gets quiet. Then turn the riddle over gently, without needing to solve it. Something small and alive, inside something that would be still without it. Feel the breath moving in a body that sits motionless. Don't push for an answer. Just let the question sit with you, the way Madhurakavi's question sat in the silence before it was answered. If you pray, you can rest in God's presence in that quiet. The bell holds the time.
The Alvars. The Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. Nammalvar is the silent one under the tamarind, who answered a riddle and then sang the Tiruvaymoli.
Your line: it will eat that, and lie there. Today, before you answer one question, let it sit in silence for a breath. Day nine hundred nine.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnavas recite Nammalvar's Tiruvaymoli in temple worship and at home, and the tamarind tree at his temple town is honored as the place where he sat.

fork.setup: you're Madhurakavi. you've followed a light a long way and found a young man sitting silent, eyes closed. what do you do?
options: leave; he clearly isn't going to talk.
ask him a riddle and wait.
shake him until he opens his eyes.
fork.reveal: he asks a riddle about a small thing born inside something dead. Nammalvar answers, and Madhurakavi becomes his disciple.

original.note: Tamil: a name for the poet-saint of the tamarind tree, said to mean our Alvar.
